The lesion was resected through a transcranial approach, and postoperative imaging showed gross total resection. Histological examination demonstrated an infiltrating high-grade glial neoplasm with brisk mitotic activity and palisading necrosis. Immunohistochemical and molecular findings, including the absence of IDH1/IDH2 mutations, supported a diagnosis of glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4. At 18 months after surgery, the patient remained alive. This case highlights a rare pattern of primary extracranial extension in GBM and suggests direct contiguous transdural invasion as a plausible route of spread in the absence of prior intervention.

items.title: Adapting the Girandole framework for cross-disciplinary social justice reflection in health professions education
items.abstract: Equality, diversity and inclusion (EDI) are increasingly embedded within the standards and strategic priorities of health professions education. However, persistent inequities, hidden curricula and differences between institutional commitments and learners' lived experiences indicate a need for approaches that move beyond policy compliance towards critical, socially informed reflection. This Perspective paper explores the cross-disciplinary adaptation of the Girandole Framework, originally developed in nursing education, for application across health professions education. The framework uses six interconnected domains—Power, Hidden Curriculum, Professional Values, Personal Values, Culture, and EDI Education and Awareness—to support examination of the individual, cultural and structural influences shaping educational and professional experiences. An exploratory cross-disciplinary workshop involving healthcare professional students informed the adaptation of the framework. Informal discussions suggested that Power, Culture, and Personal and Professional Values were readily connected to learners' experiences. In contrast, Hidden Curriculum and EDI Education and Awareness required clearer language, practical examples and additional educational scaffolding. These insights informed the refinement of the framework's reflective prompts and the development of examples relevant to nursing, pharmacy, biomedical science and transferrable to other health professions. The adapted Girandole offers a shared language through which students and educators can critically examine power relationships, informal norms, professional cultures and educational omissions. Potential future applications include clinical and laboratory placements, professionalism teaching, portfolio-based learning, interprofessional education and curriculum review; however, these applications require empirical evaluation. The framework is intended to complement established reflective models by foregrounding equity and social justice. Further student–educator co-production and empirical evaluation are needed to assess its contribution to EDI literacy, belonging, reflective practice and meaningful organisational change across health professions curricula.

items.title: Case Report: Beyond the stomach: the role of preoperative imaging in assessing regurgitation risk in patients with esophageal dilatation: a report of two cases
items.abstract: BackgroundPerioperative regurgitation of gastric or esophageal contents remains a severe complication during anesthesia. While standard fasting protocols and rapid sequence induction (RSI) are routinely employed, esophageal dilatation creates a hidden reservoir for retained food and secretions that conventional methods often fail to mitigate. Furthermore, standard gastric ultrasound lacks the field of view to detect mid-to-proximal esophageal pooling.Case presentationWe present two parallel cases emphasizing this critical challenge. Case 1 involves a 68-year-old male with esophageal carcinoma who experienced massive regurgitation of white foam during RSI, despite five days of preoperative fasting. Airway security was ultimately achieved after intensified suctioning. Case 2 describes a 42-year-old female with achalasia and marked esophageal dilatation. Informed by preoperative computed tomography (CT) and barium swallow imaging, she was safely managed using targeted pre-anesthetic conscious endoscopic suctioning, leading to an uneventful induction and peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM).ConclusionThese cases highlight the limitations of conventional fasting in managing proximal pooling. They underscore the diagnostic value of preoperative cross-sectional imaging, such as CT, when clinically indicated. Active pre-induction decompression, specifically through tailored endoscopic evacuation, is a valuable adjunctive strategy for preventing perioperative regurgitation in selected patients with megaesophagus.

items.title: Identification and validation of early vital sign trajectory subphenotypes for risk stratification in sepsis-associated liver injury: a multicenter retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: BackgroundSepsis-associated liver injury (SALI) is a serious clinical syndrome with heterogeneity in outcome among affected individuals. Physiological changes that are critical to outcome prediction are not considered in the existing system of stratification based on single-point observations. This could compromise the effectiveness of individualized treatment.ObjectiveTo develop and validate dynamic clinical subphenotypes of SALI using early vital sign trajectories.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included 1,159 patients from MIMIC-IV as the derivation cohort and 168 patients from the Second Xiangya Hospital as the external validation cohort. Early vital sign trajectories within 12 h of ICU admission were summarized as trajectory-derived features and clustered using K-means. Candidate solutions (k = 2–6) were assessed using internal clustering metrics and bootstrap stability. A four-cluster solution was retained as an exploratory partition, considering trajectory interpretability and subgroup sizes. Clinical characteristics, organ support, and mortality outcomes were compared across the identified subphenotypes.ResultsFour exploratory SALI subphenotypes with distinct early vital sign trajectories were identified, ranging from relatively stable profiles to marked hemodynamic and physiological stress. Subphenotype 3 exhibited the most stable vital signs and was associated with lower adjusted 28-day (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.56–0.97) and 90-day mortality (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.59–0.97) compared with the highest-risk Subphenotype 4. These prognostic differences were consistently replicated in the external cohort, supporting short- to intermediate-term prognostic generalizability.ConclusionEarly vital sign trajectories identified exploratory SALI groups associated with differences in 28-day and 90-day mortality. Their reproducibility, incremental prognostic value, and clinical utility require further evaluation.

items.title: Concurrent Bartholin gland and perianal abscesses in a woman: a case report of a diagnostic challenge
items.abstract: BackgroundBartholin gland abscess and perianal abscess are common suppurative infections involving anatomically adjacent regions of the female perineum. Because both conditions may present with localized pain and swelling, distinguishing their respective origins and determining the extent of infection can be challenging. The concomitant occurrence of these two abscesses is uncommon, and its diagnostic and therapeutic considerations remain poorly characterized. We report a rare case of concomitant Bartholin gland and perianal abscesses and describe the diagnostic process and multidisciplinary surgical management.Case presentationAn 18-year-old woman presented with progressive perineal and perianal pain and swelling. Pelvic computed tomography demonstrated abscess formation involving the perianal and left perineal soft tissues, and a possible communication between the two lesions was initially suspected. Emergency surgery was performed. The perianal abscess was incised and drained, and an infected anal gland was identified and excised, with bridge drainage established between the drainage incisions. Intraoperative exploration revealed no communication between the perianal abscess and the adjacent perineal lesion. Following gynecological consultation, the separate left vulvar abscess was drained and treated with Jacobi ring fistulization. Culture of the perineal abscess grew Escherichia coli, whereas the perianal abscess culture showed no bacterial growth. Follow-up magnetic resonance imaging 1 month after surgery demonstrated a cystic lesion in the anatomical region of the left Bartholin gland, supporting the Bartholin gland origin of the previously drained perineal abscess. The patient showed satisfactory clinical recovery, with complete healing of the perianal and perineal wounds at 4 months and no evidence of recurrent abscess during the available follow-up.ConclusionConcomitant Bartholin gland and perianal abscesses may be difficult to distinguish because of their overlapping clinical manifestations and anatomical proximity. Clinicians should consider the possibility of multiple independent or potentially related infectious foci and systematically evaluate adjacent anatomical regions. Careful physical examination, appropriate imaging, intraoperative assessment, and timely multidisciplinary collaboration can facilitate accurate diagnosis and individualized surgical management.

items.title: Expect the unexpected: cervical gastric-type adenocarcinoma in situ in a patient with long-standing Peutz-Jeghers syndrome — a case report and literature review
items.abstract: BackgroundPeutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline mutations in the STK11 tumor suppressor gene, associated with a significantly elevated lifetime risk of various malignancies. Gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma (G-EAC) and its precursor lesions represent one of the most challenging gynecologic manifestations due to their “deceptively bland” appearance, HPV-independent nature, and propensity to evade routine screening, often leading to delayed diagnosis and poor prognosis.Case presentationWe report a 37-year-old woman with a 30-year history of PJS, presenting with persistent watery vaginal discharge for one year. Despite negative cervical cytology, negative HPV testing, normal colposcopic findings, and inconclusive imaging, her request for hysterectomy was initially declined due to absence of definitive malignant features. The patient subsequently sought care at a tertiary referral center in Shanghai, where post-hysterectomy pathological examination unexpectedly confirmed cervical gastric-type adenocarcinoma in situ (GAS-AIS).ConclusionThis case highlights a critical message: a PJS patient with persistent watery vaginal discharge may harbor gastric-type cervical glandular neoplasia despite negative cytology, negative HPV testing, apparently normal cervical examination, and inconclusive imaging. Persistent watery discharge in this specific population should be considered a “red flag” for gastric-type lesions, which may arise from lobular endocervical glandular hyperplasia (LEGH). For PJS patients with persistent unexplained vaginal discharge, we suggest that clinical suspicion — rather than cytology or colposcopy findings — should be the primary trigger for diagnostic excisional procedures. We present a comprehensive literature review of PJS-associated G-EAC and advocate for updated surveillance protocols, including random cervical biopsies or excisional procedures in symptomatic PJS patients, regardless of colposcopic findings.

items.title: Effects of liraglutide on blood pressure and renal function in patients with type 2 diabetic nephropathy: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.abstract: ObjectivesThe effects of liraglutide on blood pressure in patients with T2DN remain unclear. This meta-analysis aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of liraglutide on blood pressure and renal function in patients with T2DN.MethodsWe conducted comprehensive searches of Web of Science, PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Elsevier ScienceDirect, CNKI, Wanfang Data, and VIP databases. Eligible studies were RCTs of ≥12 weeks’ duration evaluating liraglutide for T2DN. Two independent reviewers screened citations, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias Tool. Statistical analyses were performed in Stata 17.0 and RevMan 5.4, with effect sizes presented as RR or MD and 95% CI. The Cochrane Q test and I2 statistic were used to quantify statistical heterogeneity.ResultsThis meta-analysis included 23 RCTs involving 1,723 participants. Compared with the control group, liraglutide significantly reduced SBP [MD = −5.00, 95% CI (−7.17, −2.84)], while no significant effect was observed on DBP. In addition, liraglutide was associated with favorable changes in some renal biomarkers, as evidenced by reductions in Scr, UACR, Cys-C, BUN, and β2-MG, as well as elevations in eGFR. Improvements were also observed in glycemic control, lipid profiles, BMI, and inflammatory markers. Subgroup analyses indicated dose-dependent differences in UACR and LDL-C. In addition, both UACR and Scr were affected by intervention-regimen type, while HbA1c was affected by baseline albuminuria category. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings, and adjustment for publication bias did not alter the statistical significance of the key outcomes.ConclusionLiraglutide may be associated with favorable changes in selected BP, renal, metabolic, and inflammatory outcomes in patients with T2DN. However, further high-quality studies are needed to confirm these findings.Systematic Review Registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251232844, PROSPERO CRD420251232844.

items.title: A multi-class fundus disease classification framework based on self-supervised contrastive learning and dual-branch network
items.abstract: IntroductionFundus diseases including diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration are primary causes of blindness worldwide. Manual interpretation of retinal images is time-consuming and heavily reliant on clinical expertise. Although deep learning has shown promise in automated fundus image analysis, its performance remains highly data-dependent, requiring large amounts of expert annotations. Moreover, single-architecture models may have limited capacity to capture the diverse pathological features present in fundus images.MethodsThis study proposes a unified framework integrating self-supervised contrastive pre-training with a hybrid dual-branch architecture. Pre-training on unlabeled fundus images enables the model to learn generalizable representations, thereby reducing reliance on manual annotations. The dual-branch design combines EfficientNet-B4 for fine-grained detail extraction and MambaOut for large receptive field modeling. Their outputs are adaptively fused via a learnable cross-fusion module. A dendritic classifier is adopted to further improve classification performance. Comprehensive evaluations were conducted on two public datasets, OIHC and FIVES.ResultsOn the OIHC dataset, the proposed model achieved an F1-score of 96.32 ± 0.38% and a Kappa coefficient of 95.89 ± 0.43%. On the FIVES dataset, it attained 95.10 ± 0.54% and 93.49 ± 0.71%. The macro-average AUC exceeded 98% on both datasets. Ablation studies demonstrated the contribution of each component to the overall performance.ConclusionThis study indicates that combining self-supervised pre-training with a hybrid dual-branch architecture is a feasible approach for multi-class fundus disease classification. Interpretability analyses suggest that the model's attention regions partially overlap with clinically relevant pathological features. The framework achieved competitive performance on both datasets, showing its potential utility in scenarios with limited annotated data. Future work will focus on multi-center validation and model compression for lightweight architecture design.

items.title: Healthcare professionals’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding perioperative ischemic stroke in elderly patients
items.abstract: ObjectiveThis study aimed to evaluate healthcare professionals’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) related to perioperative ischemic stroke in elderly patients.MethodsA single-center, cross-sectional survey was conducted at a tertiary hospital in Ningxia, China, between 1 March 2025 and 1 June 2025. Healthcare professionals were recruited by convenience sampling and completed a structured questionnaire covering demographic information and their KAP regarding perioperative ischemic stroke.ResultsA total of 273 valid responses were included in the final analysis. The majority of respondents were physicians (75.46%), with most affiliated with anesthesiology departments (86.08%). The scores for knowledge, attitude, and practice were 14.41 ± 4.22 (possible range: 0–20), 36.77 ± 3.57 (possible range: 8–40), and 30.07 ± 6.51 (possible range: 8–40), respectively. Structural equation modeling showed that knowledge, attitude, and practice were positively interrelated, whereas training related to perioperative ischemic stroke and specialization in elderly patient care showed negative associations with knowledge or practice (β range: −0.287 to 0.352; all P < 0.05). Knowledge was also indirectly associated with practice through attitude, whereas training and specialization in elderly care showed negative indirect associations with attitude and practice.ConclusionHealthcare professionals exhibited inadequate perceived knowledge, positive attitudes, and suboptimal practices regarding perioperative ischemic stroke in elderly patients. These findings underscore the necessity for targeted, evidence-based educational interventions to strengthen knowledge awareness and practice-related competencies, thereby addressing the observed gaps between perceived knowledge, attitudes, and reported practices.

items.title: Amelanotic subungual melanoma becoming clinically apparent within 24 h after minor blunt trauma: a case report
items.abstract: Amelanotic subungual melanoma (ASM) is a rare variant of nail unit melanoma (NUM) lacking melanin pigmentation, frequently misdiagnosed as a benign post-traumatic or infectious lesion. To our knowledge, ASM becoming clinically apparent within 24 h following minor blunt trauma has not been reported previously. We report the case of a 66-year-old male who presented with a persistent flesh-colored nodule beneath his right thumbnail that was manifested within 24 h after minor blunt trauma caused by nail clippers. The lesion was non-tender, non-pigmented, and unresponsive to 2 weeks of antibiotic therapy. Histopathology revealed diffuse subepidermal proliferation of atypical cells with signet-ring morphology. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) demonstrated positivity for vimentin, HMB45, and Melan-A, and negativity for cytokeratin 5 (CK5) and S-100. Ki-67 was approximately 30%; Breslow thickness was 2.5 mm. Final diagnosis: ASM, AJCC stage IIA (T3aN0M0). Diagnostic excisional biopsy with a 2-mm margin was performed; sentinel lymph node biopsy of two axillary lymph nodes was negative. At 1-year follow-up, no local recurrence or distant metastasis was observed. This case demonstrates that ASM can become clinically evident within 24 h after acute trauma, likely through unmasking of a pre-existing subclinical tumor. For post-traumatic nail lesions unresponsive to antibiotics, early biopsy with a comprehensive IHC panel (including Melan-A, HMB45, and S-100) is essential.

items.title: Low arterial oxygen-content burden during the first 24 h and hospital mortality in mechanically ventilated adults: analyses of MIMIC-IV and eICU
items.abstract: BackgroundArterial oxygen content (CaO2) combines hemoglobin-bound and dissolved oxygen. A time-weighted CaO2 deficit could capture changing anemia and desaturation that a hemoglobin-only summary misses. We examined its association with hospital mortality and its added value beyond hemoglobin.MethodsIn this retrospective cohort study, we included mechanically ventilated adults from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) and eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU). The MIMIC-IV 25th percentile of the first matched CaO2 value (12.48 mL O2/dL) was prespecified as an empirical cutoff and was applied unchanged to eICU. The first-24-h burden integrated the time-weighted deficit below this cutoff. Models were adjusted for demographics and diagnosis-derived case mix. We compared CaO2 burden with hemoglobin burden calculated at the same blood-gas time points and performed landmark, measurement-coverage, severity, and post hoc peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2)-stratified analyses.ResultsBurden was available for 14,050 MIMIC-IV and 20,780 eICU stays. CaO2 was strongly correlated with hemoglobin (r = 0.965 and 0.949, respectively), which explained R2 = 0.932 and 0.901 of first-measurement CaO2 variation, respectively; median dissolved-oxygen contributions were 2.9% and 2.5%, respectively. Per 1-SD higher burden, adjusted odds ratios for hospital mortality were 1.33 (95% confidence interval 1.28–1.39) in MIMIC-IV and 1.29 (1.24–1.35) in eICU. Additional Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation adjustment attenuated the eICU estimate to 1.14 (1.10–1.19), while 24-h landmark estimates were 1.26 (1.21–1.32) and 1.19 (1.14–1.25), respectively. Cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) gains over matched hemoglobin burden were 0.006 and 0.010, respectively, and calibration was similar. In post hoc analyses, hemoglobin explained less CaO2 variation when first SpO2 was <90% (R2 = 0.787 and 0.682, respectively) than when it was ≥95% (R2 = 0.973 and 0.978, respectively); corresponding AUROC gains were 0.045 and 0.044 versus 0.002 in both databases.ConclusionIn cohorts dominated by preserved oxygen saturation, low CaO2 was predominantly an anemia-related signal, and its association with mortality was substantially attenuated by illness-severity adjustment. The burden is best viewed as a compact observational summary of the depth and duration of low arterial oxygen content, not as an independent measure of tissue oxygenation, a superior prediction model, or a treatment target.

items.title: Biomarker-guided immunotherapy in osteosarcoma: from immune microenvironment profiling to patient stratification and combination strategies
items.abstract: Osteosarcoma remains a therapeutically difficult malignancy, particularly after metastatic relapse, and immune checkpoint blockade or adoptive cell therapy has not reproduced the durable responses achieved in more immunogenic cancers. The central translational problem is not a complete absence of immune activity, but marked interpatient, intratumoral, and spatial heterogeneity in immune access, antigen presentation, myeloid suppression, stromal exclusion, and target-antigen expression. This Mini Review synthesizes recent single-cell and spatial profiling studies with tissue, circulating, and clinical biomarker evidence to define a practical framework for biomarker-guided immunotherapy. Osteosarcoma ecosystems can contain lymphoid-excluded, myeloid-dominant, angiogenic-hypoxic, checkpoint-rich, and antigen-high states that may coexist within the same patient. Consequently, programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) alone is unlikely to function as a reliable treatment-selection marker. A composite assessment integrating human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I and antigen-processing competence, CD8/regulatory T-cell topology, macrophage and myeloid-derived suppressor cell programs, vascular and extracellular-matrix barriers, and quantitative surface-antigen density is more biologically defensible. Dynamic measurements, including circulating tumor DNA, soluble B7-H3, exosomal immune signals, and serial imaging, may complement tissue profiling but remain investigational. Clinical experience with checkpoint inhibitors, antiangiogenic combinations, mifamurtide, HER2-directed approaches, and emerging B7-H3-, GD2-, ALPL-1-, CD166-, IL-11Ralpha-, and NKG2D-based cellular therapies underscores the need to match mechanism to phenotype. Prospective studies should therefore use standardized, spatially resolved, and longitudinal biomarker panels to enrich trials, distinguish prognostic from predictive effects, and adapt therapy when immune exclusion or antigen escape emerges.

items.title: Osteopathic manipulative treatment as an adjunct therapy in a pediatric patient with chronic pancreatitis and visceral hyperalgesia: a case report
items.abstract: BackgroundChronic abdominal pain arising from visceral hyperalgesia is difficult to manage, and the use of osteopathic manipulative medicine in pancreatitis-associated visceral hyperalgesia is rarely described. This case adds to the literature by highlighting a potential integrative, mechanism-informed approach for pain modulation in a complex pediatric patient.CaseA 17-year-old male with chronic pancreatitis in the setting of a heterozygous SPINK1 N34S (c.101A > G; p.Asn34Ser) variant, presented with acute-on-chronic abdominal pain severe enough to require escalating opioid therapy; imaging demonstrated calcifications, edema, and peripancreatic fluid collections. A multimodal treatment plan was initiated that included gabapentin, nortriptyline, and targeted osteopathic manipulative treatment. A secretin-enhanced MRCP obtained during a prior admission one month earlier demonstrated pancreatic calcifications, edema, and peripancreatic fluid collections. During the current hospitalization, serum lipase decreased from 979 U/L on admission to 90 U/L by hospital day 3, when gabapentin, nortriptyline, and targeted osteopathic manipulative treatment were initiated as part of a multimodal treatment plan. The patient had two sessions of osteopathic treatment and they were each associated with reductions in pain without adverse effects. As-needed opioid medications were discontinued by discharge as part of a multimodal therapy plan. The patient remained pain-free at one-month follow-up with minimal opioid use, suggesting a potential role for osteopathic manipulative medicine as part of a multimodal strategy in the treatment of chronic pancreatitis related pain. At three-month follow-up, the patient reported pain rated 4/10 occurring several times per week and subsequently underwent total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation for definitive management.ConclusionThis case describes an association between OMT and short-term pain improvement within a multimodal treatment strategy for chronic pancreatitis-related visceral pain. Although causality cannot be established from a single uncontrolled observation, the findings support further investigation of OMT as a potential adjunctive therapy in pediatric patients with chronic pancreatitis and secondary visceral hyperalgesia.

items.title: Explainable machine learning for preoperative prediction of acute kidney injury after intertrochanteric fracture surgery in older adults
items.abstract: BackgroundAcute kidney injury (AKI) is an important postoperative complication in older patients undergoing surgery for intertrochanteric femoral fracture. This study aimed to develop and internally evaluate an explainable model for preoperative AKI risk assessment.MethodsThis retrospective study included 616 patients aged ≥60 years, including 54 (8.8%) who developed postoperative AKI. Candidate predictors were processed and selected using development-cohort data, and seven machine-learning algorithms were compared. Model performance was assessed across 100 repeated stratified 70/30 partitions and by 500-repetition model-specific and complete-pipeline bootstrap analyses. Calibration, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP were used to evaluate and interpret the selected model.ResultsThe reported Naive Bayes model comprised baseline serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, chloride, uric acid, and chronic kidney disease or renal insufficiency. Across 100 repeated partitions, its mean validation AUC was 0.7231 (SD, 0.0260). The optimism-corrected AUC was 0.8004 for the fixed five-predictor Naive Bayes specification and 0.756 when the complete development pipeline was repeated; the latter analysis yielded a corrected Brier score of 0.084, calibration intercept of 0.02, and calibration slope of 1.70. In the original algorithm-comparison cohort, the observed AUC was 0.795 (95% CI, 0.698–0.892). When the first serum creatinine measurement obtained after admission was used as the alternative reference value, the number of AKI events decreased from 54 to 43 and the validation AUC was 0.706 (95% CI, 0.586–0.826).ConclusionThe model showed moderate internal discrimination across repeated partitions. Model-specific and complete-pipeline bootstrap analyses provided complementary estimates of internal optimism. The model may complement routine preoperative renal assessment while its calibration and transportability are evaluated in additional cohorts.

items.title: Clinical challenges in vaccine and monoclonal antibody development against ESCAPE pathogens: insights from EMA scientific advice procedures
items.abstract: BackgroundCombating ESCAPE pathogens (E. faecium, S. aureus, C. difficile, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa, and Enterobacteriaceae) remains a major public health concern due to their treatment resistance and immune evasion. Vaccines and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are promising solutions, yet only one mAb is licensed and no vaccine has reached that stage. To identify recurring clinical challenges, we analyzed final advice letters (FALs) issued through the European Medicines Agency's (EMA) Scientific Advice procedure.MethodsWe searched both the Paul-Ehrlich-Institut local database and the EMA database for FALs on vaccines and mAbs targeting ESCAPE pathogens. We included FALs that matched the pathogen and product criteria and addressed clinical development. We excluded those focused solely on quality, non-clinical, safety, or post-marketing aspects. From the included FALs, we extracted information across four main categories: primary endpoint, statistical analyses, study population, and study design. Regulatory responses were classified as fully, silently, partially, or not endorsed. We subsequently reviewed related clinical trial protocols to assess whether recommendations were implemented and to provide a narrative summary of changes to the development programs.ResultsWe included 14 FALs for each of the two medicine categories, related to six vaccine and 13 mAb trials. To address common challenges across the primary endpoints, regulators recommended selecting single, infection-related endpoints and emphasized precise clinical and laboratory case definitions to ensure attribution of infection to the target pathogen. They further advised on incorporating supportive evidence, such as subgroup analyses of cases or inflammation markers, direct microbiological or indirect measures (e.g., antibiotic use, hospital stay), or survival-related endpoints. Recommendations for study populations focused on refining the inclusion/exclusion criteria to identify those most likely to benefit. Regulators also advised on changes in the statistical analysis plan (mainly due to lower-than-expected incidence) and generally discouraged single pivotal trials.ConclusionThe development of vaccines and mAbs against ESCAPE pathogens is challenged by pathogen diversity, unpredictable infection rates, heterogeneous trial populations, and diagnostic uncertainty. In a field with no one-size-fits-all development pathway, early regulatory interaction and multidisciplinary disease-expert input are essential to reduce uncertainty and support robust, efficient clinical development programs.

items.title: Extensive vulvar and perianal langerhans cell histiocytosis with clinical improvement during low-dose thalidomide and topical therapy: a case report
items.abstract: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) involving the female genital region is uncommon and can closely resemble chronic inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic vulvar diseases. We report a case of a 35-year-old woman with a 6-month history of recurrent painful brownish-red plaques, nodules, erosions, and ulcerations that began in the perianal region and subsequently extended to the vulva. Topical fusidic acid only provided temporary symptomatic relief. Histopathological examination revealed epidermal erosion and crusting, acanthosis, elongated rete ridges, and a dense dermal and subcutaneous infiltrate containing numerous large histiocytes with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and focal nuclear grooves. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the lesional cells exhibited positivity for S100, CD1a, and langerin and negative for HMB45, SOX10, ALK-1A4, and BRAF V600E. Broader molecular testing for MAPK-pathway alterations was not performed, and the lesion was therefore described as BRAF V600E-immunonegative rather than genetically BRAF/MAPK wild type. The pathological diagnosis was vulvar LCH, with clinically suspected involvement of the perianal region. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) revealed an enlarged cervical lymph node, with no other abnormalities documented; its relationship to LCH could not be determined. Oral thalidomide (50 mg nightly) was subsequently administered while topical Pevisone was continued. Symptomatic improvement, particularly pain relief, was observed after 1 week, and further clinical improvement of the anogenital lesions was documented at 3 months. Because both therapies were used concomitantly, the independent contribution of thalidomide could not be determined. This case underscores the diagnostic challenges associated with anogenital LCH and documents short-term clinical improvement during a low-dose thalidomide-containing regimen without establishing thalidomide monotherapy efficacy. It also highlights the necessity for biopsy, comprehensive systemic evaluation, and ongoing follow-up.

items.title: Skeletal muscle enhancer programming of intrinsic cardiorespiratory fitness
items.abstract: Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is a heritable trait associated with improved metabolic health and longevity. Integrating 546 transcriptomic and epigenomic profiles from skeletal muscle of 128 genetically heterogeneous rats selectively bred for high and low running capacity (HCR and LCR), a model that mirrors CRF-associated traits in humans, we identify a distributed enhancer architecture underlying their divergent transcriptomes. Line-divergent alleles were concentrated in distal enhancers: those more active in HCR were enriched for ETS-family transcription factor motifs and positively linked to hundreds of mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and angiogenesis genes, whereas those more active in LCR were enriched for Mef2 motifs and negatively linked to these genes. In 426 genotype, gene expression, and chromatin accessibility profiles from an independent HCRxLCR F2 population (n=147), we validated thousands of these genetic effects. Thus, heritable CRF reflects many enhancers cumulatively tuning energy metabolism and oxygen delivery, providing a molecular basis for variation in CRF.
items.authors: Weitzel, A. M.; Orchard, P.; Evans, C.; Manickam, N.; Treutelaar, M. K.; Britton, S. L.; Koch, L. G.; Li, J. Z.; Parker, S. C. J.; Burant, C. F.

items.title: Design of Orthogonal Far-Red, Orange and Green Fluorophore-binding Proteins for Multiplex Imaging
items.abstract: Fluorescent proteins have transformed biological imaging, yet their limited photostability and brightness restrict their applications. We used deep learning-based de novo protein design methods to design binders to three bright, stable and cell-permeable dyes spanning the imaging spectrum: JF657 (far red), JF596 (orange-red) and JF494 (green). We obtain highly specific dye-binding proteins with low nanomolar affinities for the intended target; a crystal structure of one binder confirms close resemblance to the design model. Simultaneous labeling of mammalian cells expressing three dye-specific binders at different subcellular compartments demonstrates the utility in multiplex imaging. We further expand the functionality of the binder by incorporating an active site that carries out nucleophilic aromatic substitution to form a covalent linkage with the dye, and develop split versions which reconstitute fluorescence at subcellular locations where both halves are present towards monitoring in-cell protein interactions and chemically induced dimerization. Our designed high affinity and specificity dye binders open up new opportunities for multiplexed biological imaging.
items.authors: Tran, L.; Klein, S.; Sharma, S.; Juergens, D.; Decarreau, J.; Liu, B.; Wang, Y.; Bera, A. K.; Kang, A.; Woods, J.; Joyce, E.; Vafeados, D. K.; Roullier, N.; Chen, W.; Lee, G. R.; Lavis, L. D.; Mahamid, J.; An, L.; Baker, D.

items.title: Dysfunctional effector programming in Foxp3-ΔE2 Tregs promotes enhanced CD8+ T cell responses
items.abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) prevent autoimmunity through suppressive functions largely programmed by the transcription factor FOXP3. Humans express two major alternatively spliced isoforms of FOXP3: a full-length version containing all coding exons (FOXP3-FL) and a version lacking Exon 2 (FOXP3-{Delta}E2). Sole FOXP3-{Delta}E2 expression causes lethal IPEX syndrome, indicating that FOXP3 Exon 2 is essential for full Treg function. Here, we used Foxp3-{Delta}E2 mice to determine how Foxp3 Exon 2 impacts the functional differentiation of Tregs at homeostasis and during inflammation. Analysis of central and effector Foxp3-{Delta}E2 Treg populations revealed dysfunctional effector Treg programming, including reduced expression of IL-2 receptor subunits, CTLA-4, and tissue-homing chemokine receptors. During influenza infection, reduced IL-2 regulation by Foxp3-{Delta}E2 Tregs and decreased Foxp3-{Delta}E2 Treg localization to the T cell zone during priming contributed to enhanced acute and memory CD8+ T cell responses. Thus, dysfunctional effector Treg programming by the Foxp3-{Delta}E2 isoform impairs suppressive function, resulting in failure to restrain CD8+ T cells and aberrant immune responses.
items.authors: Weinstein, K. N.; Bishop, Z. H.; Shamskhou, E. A.; Barry, F. N.; Verdezoto, G.; de Leon, M.; Albe, J. R.; Koval, A.; Zhou, B.; Domeier, P. P.; Gerner, M. Y.; Campbell, D. J.; Ziegler, S. F.

items.title: Combined High Fat and Viral Insults in Pregnancy Disrupt Specific Placental Nutrient Transporter Systems in Mice
items.abstract: The placenta adapts to support nutrient transport to meet the demands of the growing fetus. Maternal obesity and viral infection are associated with adverse fetoplacental development. How co-exposure affects placental morphology and nutrient transport across gestation remains unclear. We hypothesise that co-exposure would have a greater impact on placental morphology and nutrient transporter expression than either of the exposures alone. C57BL/6J mice were fed a control (CON) or high-fat (HF) diet before and throughout pregnancy and exposed to poly(I:C) or vehicle at gestational days (GD) 12.5, 15.5, or 18.5. Placental morphology, folate and fatty acid transporter mRNA expression and localisation were evaluated by haematoxylin and eosin staining, immunohistochemistry (reported as % immunoreactivity (ir)-area stained), and qPCR, respectively. At GD12.5, HF diet associated with reduced junctional zone (JZ) area and increased maternal blood space, followed by reduced fetal blood space at GD15.5 and increased JZ and labyrinth zone (LZ) area size by GD18.5. HF diet and viral infection independently associated with increased placental Fat/Cd36 mRNA expression at GD12.5. However, HF diet and infection associated with increased ir-FR- while HF diet alone decreased ir-PCFT at GD12.5. By GD15.5, HF diet associated with reduced placental ir-FR- but increased ir-PCFT. At GD18.5, infection associated with reduced Rfc1 mRNA expression. HF diet and infection associated with greater prevalence of SGA and LGA fetuses, particularly at GD18.5. Obesity and infection independently and jointly disrupted placental morphology and nutrient transporter expression in a zone- and gestational age-specific manner, with consequences for fetal growth across gestation.
items.authors: Ferraz, T.; Cardoso, L.; Mohammadkhani, S.; Bloise, E.; Connor, K.

items.title: Structural features and conservation of the lncRNA HOTAIR in primates
items.abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate diverse cellular processes and are frequently implicated in disease, but their functional mechanisms often remain elusive. One such lncRNA, HOTAIR (Hox transcript antisense intergenic RNA), is a ~2.1 kb mammalian transcript whose overexpression promotes invasion and metastasis in breast cancer. However, the mechanisms by which HOTAIR influences gene regulation in cancer are poorly understood. To approach this problem through a structural lens, we predicted the full-length in cellulo secondary structure of HOTAIR using chemical probing in a metastatic breast cancer cell line. The resulting structure shows that HOTAIR adopts a multidomain architecture and has local structural features unique to the cellular context. Comparison between in vitro and in cellulo chemical probing identifies regions of differential accessibility that may indicate context-dependent molecular interactions or folding. Conservation analyses further reveal that HOTAIR is conserved across primates with evidence of structural covariation in specific domains. Together, these results provide a roadmap for future mechanistic studies of structure-function relationships in HOTAIR and its contribution to gene regulation in cancer.
items.authors: Perry, Z. R.; Beeram, A.; Lee, L.; Pyle, A. M.

items.title: Synthetic genetic circuits that count developmental cues in plant roots
items.abstract: Plants explore soil environments through their roots, which branch repeatedly to access water and soil-borne nutrients. In many plants, root branches are generated by repeated developmental programs and molecular analyses have not identified markers that distinguish primary from later root branches. Consequently, efforts to engineer plant roots for improved water or nutrient acquisition are limited to changes that affect the entire root system. Here, we developed synthetic genetic circuits to count repeating root development cues and enable differential gene expression in successive root branches of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. The circuits use a root primordium-specific promoter to express large serine recombinases, which irreversibly invert segments of DNA each time a new lateral root is initiated. This converts repeating rounds of root formation into distinct, heritable DNA states. Because root branch specification and outgrowth occur over a ~2 day period, we tested circuit designs for their ability to count long-duration input pulses and developed an architecture that produces distinct fluorescence outputs in primary, secondary, and tertiary roots. By linking repeated developmental cues to distinct genetic outputs, synthetic genetic circuits that count enable root system engineering at the resolution of individual branches and offer a general strategy for dissecting developmental processes that rely on repeated signals.
items.authors: Choi, S.; Brophy, J. A. N.

items.title: Molecular sterics guide tmRNA translocation on the ribosome
items.abstract: Translation of defective mRNA transcripts can lead to the formation of stalled ``non-stop'' ribosome complexes. To rescue these ribosomes, bacteria have evolved a mechanism called trans-translation that is mediated by transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA) and small protein B (SmpB). During the translocation step of trans-translation, the stalled mRNA is ejected and the reading frame found in the mRNA-like domain (MLD) of tmRNA is loaded into the mRNA channel. The ribosome then translates the new template, thereby tagging the nascent protein for degradation. While structures of tmRNA-SmpB on the ribosome have been available for years, little is known about the molecular factors that govern the dynamics of tmRNA translocation. Here, we use an energetically smooth model (i.e. SMOG) to simulate translocation of tmRNA-SmpB, which reveals that the structure of the ribosome gives rise to a preferred sequence of conformational substeps. Specifically, the tRNA-like domain (TLD) translocates, then the MLD loads, and finally the C-terminal tail of SmpB rearranges. These steps are interdependent and associated with a range of sterically-induced barriers that regulate the kinetics. This provides a structural and energetic framework for understanding, and ultimately controlling, the dynamics of trans-translation.
items.authors: Wanes, G.; Keiler, K. C.; Dunham, C. M.; Whitford, P. C.

items.title: Amide I kurtosis maps cardiac amyloid in human tissue by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy
items.abstract: Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by deposits of misfolded proteins in the heart and can lead to heart failure. Histological confirmation typically involves staining tissue sections with Congo red and examining them under polarized light for apple-green birefringence; however, achieving an interpretable, label-free, and observer-independent assessment remains challenging. Here we show that Pearson kurtosis of channel intensities within the amide I window provides an interpretable, fitting-free contrast for cardiac amyloid in unstained human cardiac tissue sections from ten participants imaged by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS). In a discovery participant, high-kurtosis regions corresponded with Congo red-positive tissue in two CARS-histology pairs of adjacent sections (descriptive spatial AUCs, 0.79 and 0.73). Across 15 fields from nine additional participants, field-level kurtosis values did not overlap between severe-deposition and Congo red-negative tissue fields. Among the descriptors examined, kurtosis showed the largest standardized participant-level separation. Exploratory multivariate curve resolution yielded a deposit-associated component with aromatic-residue features shared with reagent transthyretin. In one field from the discovery participant, the second harmonic generation (SHG) signal, acquired simultaneously with CARS, showed a broadly inverse spatial pattern relative to the amide I kurtosis map, revealing distinct tissue-architectural contrast. Together, these findings support a potential label-free approach to detecting cardiac amyloid deposits that combines amide I kurtosis derived from broadband CARS with SHG-derived architectural contrast.
items.authors: Ota, K.; Chen, T.-H.; Yamaguchi, T.; Otsubo, T.; Murakami, Y.; Masaki, M.; Leproux, P.; Suzuki, R.; Node, K.; Kano, H.

items.title: Potassium modulates Phytophthora zoospore motility and flagellar beating through dose-dependent effects
items.abstract: Biflagellate zoospores are critical agents in the spread of Phytophthora spp., plant pathogens causing major agronomic and economic losses worldwide. These motile cells navigate soil water films toward plant roots using taxis triggered by environmental cues. Here, we investigate how potassium modulates zoospore motility by analyzing trajectory and flagellar beating parameters across KCl concentrations. Using high-speed imaging, we apply kymograph analysis and Fourier transform of the cell body direction over time to quantify flagellar dynamics, while low-speed imaging provides trajectory characteristics. Our results demonstrate that increasing potassium concentration significantly reduces swimming speed while enhancing directional changes. We establish a direct correlation between altered swimming speed and changes in flagellar beating parameters. Our findings indicate that potassium differentially affects anterior and posterior flagella beating. Furthermore, potassium exerts multiple effects, influencing beat amplitude, wave propagation speed and direction- change frequency. This reveals potassium as a key modulator of zoospore motility, triggering a shift from exploratory swimming to confined, reoriented movement. By uncovering the biomechanical responses of zoospores to potassium, this study advances our understanding of how surrounding signals regulate pathogen dispersal in the environment.
items.authors: Lupatelli, C. A.; ATTARD, A.; Galiana, E.; Cohen, C.; Thomen, P.; Noblin, X.

items.title: STRUCTURAL AND MOLECULAR DYNAMICS ANALYSIS OF HUMAN β-DEFENSIN 1 VARIANTS REVEALS DISTINCT PERTURBATION SIGNATURES
items.abstract: Human {beta}-defensin 1 (hBD-1) is a small, disulfide-constrained antimicrobial peptide produced predominantly in the kidney and urogenital tract, where it contributes to epithelial innate defense. Genetic variation in the gene encoding hBD-1 has been associated with altered expression levels and susceptibility to infections, including infection following solid organ transplantation, yet the molecular consequences of coding substitutions in the active, mature form remain largely undefined. Here, we integrate conventional genomics, protein bioinformatics, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics to investigate the molecular consequences of 93 human-observed hBD-1 missense variants. Evaluation of hBD-1 missense variants across sequence-, structure-, and dynamics-based dimensions reveals variant-specific molecular perturbation signatures that complement conventional and static biophysical predictions. By treating naturally occurring substitutions as a perturbation series across a compact defensin scaffold, this study identifies multiple molecular routes through which sequence variation can remodel an endogenous antimicrobial peptide and prioritizes variants for direct structure-function testing. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for investigating how naturally occurring hBD-1 variation may influence peptide behavior and, ultimately, antimicrobial function.
items.authors: Fogarty, R. J.; Urrutia, R.; Pinto e Vairo, F.; Hong, J. C.; Lomberk, G.

items.title: Cross-linker binding strength influences actin assembly microstructure and myosin II driven remodeling
items.abstract: The actin cytoskeleton is a self-assembled material that acts as the mechanical scaffold of the cell. Within the cell, protein cross-linkers organize actin filaments into assemblies with various microstructures that support distinct physiological functions. These protein cross-linkers differ in structural features. To decouple the role of individual cross-linker properties in actin assembly microstructure and mechanics, we synthesize programmable cross-linkers using a DNA linker coupled to binding domains. We find that high affinity cross-linkers induce actin bundling, while low affinity cross-linkers form actin networks. Myosin II motors remodel and contract all cross-linked networks tested in distinct ways from uncross-linked networks. We find that networks with high affinity cross-linkers have different myosin induced dynamics than networks with low affinity cross-linkers. This research expands our understanding of how cells regulate their mechanics and microstructures, while also providing insight towards the structure-property relationship in complex soft materials.
items.authors: Feigeles, C. A.; Janquart, M.; Armstrong, V.; Weirich, K. L.

items.title: Synthesis and characterization of NIR fluorescent BODIPY-Xanthene hybrid dyes
items.abstract: The development of NIR fluorescent dyes with favorable optical properties is of great importance especially for applications within the field of optical imaging. In this study, we report the design, synthesis and photophysical characterization of novel BODIPY-Xanthene hybrid dyes obtained via Knoevenagel condensation between an asymmetrical BODIPY core and the functionalized xanthene aldehydes intermediates. The synthesized dyes ex-hibit absorption (667 nm) and emission bands (720-722 nm) within the NIR region. Detailed UV-Vis and fluo-rescence studies were performed and molar extinction coefficients and stokes shifts also calculated. Moreover, findings highlighting the influence of structural modifications on the optical behavior of the hybrid dyes and their potential utility in optical imaging applications are reported.
items.authors: Nigianni, G.; Katsamakas, S.; Alexandratou, E.; Prousis, K. C.

items.title: Quantification of cellular contributions to multi-cellular pattern formation
items.abstract: Multi-cellular pattern formation is a key process in organism development, regeneration, and disease. Such multi-cellular patterns include, for instance, cell density and gene expression patterns. Here, we develop a cell-track-based method that quantifies how much individual cellular processes contribute to the emergence of large-scale patterns. These cellular processes include changes in cellular expression levels, cell motion, cell divisions, and apoptosis. We validate our method using synthetic data, before demonstrating it on two sets of experimental data. Our method is purely geometric and does not require any mechanistic assumptions about the underlying pattern-forming processes, making it very generic and robust. It thus enables unbiased, data-driven study of the mechanisms driving pattern formation across a broad class of systems.
items.authors: Estavoyer, M.; Zhao, M. L.; Merkel, M.

items.title: Microscopic collisions govern macroscopic aerotactic spreading through emergent transport coefficients
items.abstract: Collective migration is often attributed to complex cell-cell communication, yet coordinated multicellular dynamics can also emerge in organisms lacking social interactions. Continuum descriptions successfully capture such behaviors but generally rely on phenomenological transport coefficients whose microscopic origin remains elusive. Here we show that these coefficients emerge from cell-cell collisions and can be independently determined from experiments. We investigate the aerotactic dispersal of confined colonies of the solitary amoeba Acanthamoeba castellanii, in which oxygen consumption continuously reshapes the local environment to generate self-organized guidance cues. Combining quantitative videomicroscopy, oxygen mapping with phosphorescent sensing films, and oxygen-controlled microfluidics, we directly measure both the oxygen landscape and the aerotactic response governing colony expansion. We then develop a Patlak-Keller-Segel (PKS) -type drift-diffusion model whose transport coefficients are entirely determined from independent experiments and microscopic-to-macroscopic modeling approach, without adjustable parameters. The model quantitatively reproduces the observed dynamics, including the coexistence of a fast ballistic front and a trailing transient accumulation band. We show that both diffusion and aerotactic transport are modulated by the same collision-controlled mechanism through density-dependent changes in cell persistence. More generally, our results establish transport coefficients as measurable emergent properties bridging microscopic cell dynamics and macroscopic collective behavior, providing a predictive framework for oxygen-guided migration in living active matter.
items.authors: Ghazi, N.; Hirose, S.; Funamoto, K.; Calvez, V.; Anjard, C.; Cochet-Escartin, O.; Demircigil, M.; RIEU, J.-P.

items.title: A deep learning-generated hASIC1a miniprotein inhibitor confers neuroprotection in stroke
items.abstract: Ion channels remain notoriously recalcitrant drug targets despite their extensive pathophysiological significance. Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are proton-gated cation channels that cause neuronal death when excessively activated, such as during ischaemic stroke. This acidosis-driven injury pathway remains unchallenged by existing therapeutics. Here we generate two de novo designed hASIC1a-specific miniproteins by developing a platform that integrates computational miniprotein design, high-throughput automated patch clamp screening, biophysical and structural characterisation, and in vivo validation. We identify a subtype-selective hASIC1a inhibitor, Denasin1, which achieves near-complete inhibition with nanomolar potency. Denasin1 is disordered in solution but adopts the computationally predicted helix-turn-helix fold when bound to the extracellular acidic pocket of hASIC1a. Crucially, Denasin1 reduces infarct volume by > 50% in a murine model of ischaemic stroke. We thereby establish our de novo design platform as a route to develop potent and selective ion channel modulators.
items.authors: Sormann, J.; Epitropaki, K.; Vicino, M. F.; Fjorbak, C. L.; Pugh, C. F.; Lang, B.; Beyer, E. K.; Comaposada-Baro, R.; Hink, F.; Friis, S.; Usher, S. G.; Cai, C.; Autzen, H. E.; Rogers, J. M.; Pless, S.

items.title: Structural Insights into the Expanded Substrate Scope of a Cysteine-Dependent Hydrolase from Rhodococcus opacus for Polyethylene, Polypropylene, and Polystyrene Biodegradation
items.abstract: Microplastic pollution from homopolymers such as polypropylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), and polyethylene (PE) poses growing health and environmental concerns, highlighting the need for robust polymer-degrading biocatalysts. We previously identified a naturally occurring cysteine-dependent hydrolase (CsdH) from Rhodococcus opacus, featuring a unique Cys160-Lys127-Asp39 catalytic triad and providing a novel mechanism for polyethylene terephthalate (PET) degradation. In this study, we have determined crystal structures of CsdH in complex with PP, PS, PE, and styrene and demonstrated the potential of the enzyme to directly degrade these homopolymers into their respective low molecular weight degradation products using LC-MS. Structural analysis reveals that the enzyme retains a conserved principal access tunnel while undergoing subtle substrate-dependent changes to accommodate different substrates. The enzyme exhibited broad plastic degradation activity with the highest weight loss observed for PE, followed by PP and PS. SEM analysis reveals surface roughness, cracks and grooves, confirming polymer degradation. Further, these results corroborate through FTIR and TGA analysis. These findings establish a strong foundation for enzyme engineering and aim at developing efficient microplastic degradation.
items.authors: Aggarwal, S.; Singh, S.; Kayastha, A.; Aggarwal, D.; Jangid, K.; Shakib, M.; Singh, D.; Sharma, A. K.; Kumar, P.

items.title: A transient third metal ion shapes the catalytic cycle of a group I intron ribozyme
items.abstract: The self-splicing group I intron ribozyme from Tetrahymena thermophillia (THr) is a prototypical example of how RNA overcomes its limited chemical repertoire to form complex, negatively charged junctions and catalyze chemical reactions. Despite over 30 years of biochemical and structural characterization, questions still remain regarding the requirements for THr catalysis that may inform structure based drug design against group I introns, as well as the use of THr as an RNA editing tool. Recent cryo-EM structures have provided an unprecedented window into the first and second steps of splicing, enabling detailed mechanistic investigation at the atomistic level. In this work, we leverage solvation theory, molecular dynamics, alchemical free energy simulations, and machine learning accelerated QM/MM to probe outstanding questions related to 1) the role of a possible third Mg2+ binding in the active site, 2) differences in catalytic requirements between Gexo cofactors and between the first and second steps of splicing, 3) the potential role of an acid or base, and 4) restrictions on the identity of the 5' exon splice site nucleotide, U(-1). We propose that a transient, cofactor dependent, interaction with a third metal participates in the first step, while a higher affinity interaction with this third ion is required in the second step. We also propose that the presence of a phosphate on the Gexo in the first step, and analogously the G{omega} in the second step, forms a metal ion binding site not present when guanosine is bound. Finally, we propose and computationally test design modifications of G22 (isofunctional substitutions of 2,6-diaminopurine that tune the pKa at the N1 position) that we predict will enable the accommodation of C(-1) in a crucial wobble-like pair at physiological pH. This design would provide a potential strategy for expanding the sequence space accessible to programmable trans-splicing ribozymes in RNA editing applications.
items.authors: McCarthy, E.; Ekesan, S.; Giese, T. J.; Du, Y.; Barletta, G. P.; Götz, A. W.; Piccirilli, J. A.; York, D. M.

items.title: Physical Basis Of pKa Shift For Ionizable Lipids In An LNP-like Environment
items.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading drug delivery platform for mRNA or other nucleic acid-based therapeutics. LNP platforms are typically composed of ionizable aminolipids, phospholipids, sterols, and lipids tagged with polyethylene glycol. The ionizable aminolipids are typically cationic at low pH, allowing them to encapsulate negatively charged mRNA. The pH at which the ionizable head groups change charge states, the apparent pKa, is crucial to understand the characteristics and formulation of LNP. However, this is difficult to measure as the apparent pKa differs from the pKa of the aminolipids in bulk solution due to the complex chemical and charge environment. In this study, we use molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with alchemical free energy perturbation to calculate the pKa shift as a function of lipid composition, treating LNP-like and vesicle-like environments. Our results show that the pH-dependent structure of the systems affects the trends in pKa shifts in complex ways, driven by factors including surface electrostatics and lipid internalization. Our all-atom simulation protocol allows us to efficiently estimate the apparent pKa of LNP-like models formed with novel ionizable aminolipids and estimate how it will change with composition.
items.authors: Sharma, A.; Sur, S.; Grossfield, A.

items.title: Crowding governs resistance confinement and guides the improvement of adaptive therapy in a 2D melanoma model system
items.abstract: The emergence of treatment resistant mutants is one of the primary contributors to therapy failure in cancer. Evolution-based adaptive therapies aim to exploit the competition between sensitive and resistant cells to prolong therapeutic control. However, in the densely packed tissues of solid tumors, competition is not only determined by cell-intrinsic factors but also a result of local physical interactions between neighboring cells. The successful development of physics-informed adaptive therapies therefore hinges upon the bottom-up integration of tissue mechanics and experimentally grounded models of tumor evolution. Here, we show how population-level treatment response emerges from mechanical interactions between individual cells. Combining genetically tailored therapy-mimicry experiments in spatially structured 2D melanoma colonies with mechanistic, particle-based tissue simulations as digital twins in a real-to-sim-to-real framework, we reveal how treatment-induced changes in mechanical crowding shape a cascade of resistance expansion, spatial competitive escape, and consequent therapy failure. We then link these underlying physical mechanisms to population-level observables in an abstracted mathematical model for reinforcement-learning-based therapy optimization and a distilled treatment-decision-heuristic, which we test experimentally. Together, our results identify mechanical crowding and escape as governing principles of resistance-mediated therapy failure in solid tumours and provide a basis for mechanistically informed, evolution-based treatment strategies.
items.authors: Kayser, J.; Eiche, M.; Fischer, E. F.; Smith, A.-S.; Milas, M.; Citak, T.; Aif, S.

items.title: Grow2Fold: mapping heterogeneous developmental growth to human brain folding
items.abstract: Cortical folding emerges through complex developmental processes, yet what organizes these processes into the characteristic folding patterns of the human brain remains unclear. Here, we developed an imaging-informed whole-brain modeling framework, Grow2Fold, that integrates developmental cortical regionalization, quantitative growth characterization, and mechanics-guided simulation to investigate how cortical growth shapes brain folding patterns. Using 836 fetal and neonatal MRI sessions from 747 participants spanning 21-45 postmenstrual weeks, we identified a reproducible and hierarchical spatiotemporal organization of cortical expansion characterized by coordinated regional growth trajectories. Rapid expansion occurs earlier around peri-central territories and progressively shifts toward frontal, parietal, and temporal association cortices. We encoded these imaging-derived trajectories into region- and age-specific growth laws and incorporated them into anatomically realistic whole-brain mechanical models. The resulting simulations recapitulate major sulcal landmarks and characteristic folding development across global and regional morphological measures. Comparing regional and uniform growth, we find that differential growth drives cortical instability, while heterogeneous developmental growth organizes this instability into anatomically recognizable folding patterns. Combined with subject-specific anatomy, these population-informed growth laws reproduce individualized longitudinal folding trajectories. Together, our results identify spatiotemporally patterned developmental growth as a key spatial constraint on cortical morphogenesis and establish a quantitative bridge from developmental imaging, through mechanical instability, to anatomically organized folding.
items.authors: Hou, J.; Solhtalab, A.; Jiang, K.; Gu, B.; Li, T.; Chen, X.; Wu, T.; Song, K.; Liu, Y.; Song, W.; zhu, D.; Liu, T.; Kuhl, E.; Li, G.; Razavi, M. J.; Wang, X.

items.title: CryoFAST: A Fab-Aided Cryo-EM Workflow for High-Resolution Structure Determination of Sub-50-kDa Protein Targets
items.abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) plays an increasingly important role in structure-based drug discovery (SBDD) by revealing target protein-ligand interactions at the molecular level, but its application has largely focused on large- and medium-sized protein complexes. Many therapeutically important targets are smaller than 50 kDa and remain highly challenging for cryo-EM analysis because of low signal-to-noise ratios and difficulties in particle alignment. Here, we describe cryoFAST, an integrated workflow that couples ligand-compatible Fab discovery and structure-guided computational maturation with biochemical triage, fiducial-complex assembly, and single-particle cryo-EM. Through phage-display screening and/or AI-guided design, we developed high-affinity Fab binders of approximately 50 kDa that stabilize the target without disrupting ligand-target interactions and then assembled Fab-target complexes for cryo-EM analysis. Using the therapeutically relevant extracellular domain (~20 kDa) of interleukin-4 receptor (IL-4R) as a proof of concept, we determined its cryo-EM structure at 2.74 Angstrom resolution and established a framework for elucidating ligand-binding modes. This workflow provides a practical, efficient, and potentially broadly applicable route to the structural characterization of small protein targets that are otherwise challenging to study. By extending the applicability of cryo-EM to high-value but technically challenging small targets, cryoFAST may open new opportunities for structure-based drug discovery.
items.authors: Li, X.; Deng, S.; Li, W.; Qian, Y.; Li, Y.; Du, J.; Li, L.; Qian, D.

items.title: Structural Basis for Near Infrared Absorption and Noncanonical Photoisomerization in Neorhodopsin
items.abstract: In retinal proteins, light absorption leads to a double bond isomerization of the chromophore, followed by conformational relaxations that drive functional protein rearrangements. The balance between photoisomerization and radiative or non-radiative decays of the excited state is adjusted to the demands of the respective photoreceptor function. The molecular determinants controlling the excited state processes remain poorly understood and are the focus of this combined crystallographic, spectroscopic, and theoretical work on the recently discovered neorhodopsin (NeoR). NeoR exhibits a highly red-shifted and fluorescent dark state and selectively photoisomerizes from all-trans to 7-cis. We show that the local electrostatic environment reduces the negative charge density near the Schiff base and suppresses torsional motion around the canonical C13=C14 isomerization site of microbial rhodopsins. Instead, the chromophore-binding pocket permits only low-efficiency C7=C8 isomerization, accompanied by polyene inversion, {beta}-ionone ring displacement, and Schiff base deprotonation. Consequently, unlike other retinal photoreceptors, NeoR undergoes structural changes localized near the {beta}-ionone ring.
items.authors: Kovalev, K.; Boehlke, B.; Nag, P.; Grosse, M.; Kraskov, A.; Katz, S.; Hildebrandt, P.; Bartl, F.; Schapiro, I.; Hegemann, P.; Broser, M.

items.title: Adipose Tissue Pericellular Fibrosis, Weight Loss and Features of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease after Bariatric Surgery
items.abstract: Introduction: Adipose tissue fibrosis has been associated with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and suboptimal weight loss after bariatric surgery. The objective was to characterize changes in adipose tissue fibrosis and extracellular matrix (ECM) components in adipose tissues from two abdominal fat compartments, subcutaneous and omental, in response to bariatric surgery; and determine the effect of weight loss on the association between adipose tissue fibrosis and MASLD feature changes with weight loss. Methods: Liver and adipose tissue biopsy samples were obtained before and after weight loss from patients who underwent two-stage bariatric surgery. Adipose tissue pericellular fibrosis was evaluated histologically with picrosirius red staining for collagen quantification and normalized to adipocyte count per microscope field. Transcript levels of ECM remodeling and inflammatory genes were measured by RNA sequencing in subcutaneous adipose tissue pre- and post-surgery. Results: At baseline, adipose tissue pericellular fibrosis did not associate with MASLD features, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis or hepatic fibrosis in patients with severe obesity. Changes in liver histology after surgery were unrelated to changes in adipose tissue fibrosis. Transcripts for most genes involved in ECM remodeling and inflammation were downregulated in subcutaneous fat one year after bariatric surgery. Omental, but not subcutaneous, adipose tissue fibrosis decreased after surgery when adjusted for cell number (mean {+/-} SD: 0.41 {+/-} 0.12 vs 0.32 {+/-} 0.08 {micro}m2/cell, p<0.005). Higher subcutaneous adipose tissue fibrosis correlated with reduced weight loss (estimate {+/-} SE: -2.04 {+/-} 0.99, p<0.05) and BMI loss (-0.73 {+/-} 0.35, p<0.05), while increased omental adipose tissue fibrosis after weight loss was associated with worsening hepatic fibrosis (0.31 {+/-} 0.14, p<0.05). Conclusion: In individuals with severe obesity undergoing bariatric surgery, adipose tissue fibrosis is poorly correlated with MASLD features. Notably, pericellular fibrosis in subcutaneous abdominal, but not omental, adipose tissue was associated with a reduced weight-loss response to surgery.
items.authors: Tremblay, E.-J.; de Toro Martin, J.; Lebel, S.; Couture, C.; Lajeunesse-Trempe, F.; Maltais-Payette, I.; Ostinelli, G.; Vohl, M.-C.; Biertho, L.; Mauriege, P.; Tchernof, A.

items.title: An AI-Enabled Translational Drug Discovery Framework for NALCN Channelopathy: From High-Throughput Screening to Therapeutic Candidate
items.abstract: Background: More than 90% of rare diseases lack an approved therapy, partly reflecting economic barriers in developing treatments for small patient populations. A common bottleneck is costly and resource-intensive hit-to-lead prioritization. Congenital contractures of the limbs and face, hypotonia, and developmental delay (CLIFAHDD) is an ultra-rare neurodevelopmental disease often caused by de novo gain-of-function variants in the sodium leak channel NALCN, with no approved treatments. Methods: We developed a cost and resource-efficient, AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic high-throughput screening (HTS), structural biology foundation models for hit-to-lead prioritization, and orthogonal experimental validation. We applied this framework for drug repurposing to identify NALCN inhibitors as therapeutic candidates for CLIFAHDD. We screened ~1,200 approved drugs using a fluorescence-based membrane potential assay in doxycycline-inducible HEK293 cells stably expressing the NALCN channelosome. Boltz-2 modeling predicted binding affinity and mode to prioritize hits. Lead repurposing candidates were selected by a multidisciplinary expert review panel. Lead candidates were evaluated using patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells expressing wild-type or CLIFAHDD-associated NALCN variants, primary mouse hippocampal neurons, and a C. elegans NALCN gain-of-function model. Results: HTS identified 11 candidate NALCN inhibitors. Boltz-2 prioritized candidates based on predicted binding affinity and predicted binding within the NALCN pore, consistent with a direct pore-blocking mechanism. Aprepitant emerged as the lead candidate after multidisciplinary evaluation based on its predicted mechanism, pharmacologic properties, blood-brain barrier penetration, established safety profile, and regulatory approval in children and adults. Patch-clamp electrophysiology confirmed partial inhibition of NALCN-mediated sodium leak currents in HEK293 cells (IC50;=2.22 M), with comparable potency against Cav3.1 (IC50=1.63 M). In primary mouse hippocampal neurons, aprepitant reduced sodium leak currents, hyperpolarized resting membrane potential, and decreased spontaneous firing. Aprepitant rescued hyperlocomotor and dystonic phenotypes in a C. elegans gain-of-function NALCN model. There was notable concordance between AI-predicted hits, phenotypic screening hits, and experimental validation. Conclusion: These findings identify aprepitant as a lead therapeutic candidate for CLIFAHDD, and establish an AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic screening, structural modeling, and experimental validation for NALCN channelopathies. This scalable and resource-conscious strategy may accelerate hit-to-lead prioritization and drug discovery for rare and ultra-rare diseases lacking effective therapies.
items.authors: Thongsepee, N.; Tanner, J. A.; Polusani, S.; Typou, A.; Clanton, N. A.; Holmes, B. B.; Lory, P.; Dwyer, D. S.; Zhou, D.; Monteil, A.; Yuan, Y.

items.title: Mechanistic simulation identifies predictive dose-dependent biomarkers of propofol anesthesia
items.abstract: Understanding how receptor-level modulation reorganizes large-scale brain circuits remains a central challenge in neuropharmacology. Here we introduce a multiscale mechanistic model with explicit core-matrix thalamocortical architecture to examine how propofol reorganizes brainwide activity from individual receptors to systems-level circuits. Crucially, the model did not involve machine learning or statistical fitting to pre-existing anesthesia data. We use the model to simulate the multi-scale effects of propofol, which range from modulation of individual synaptic conductances to widespread alterations of neural spiking, field potentials, and coherence. Without requiring any training on task-specific data, our simulation of sensory processing in a standard auditory oddball paradigm matches independent data from anesthetized and awake behaving macaques. The same simulation, unmodified, also reproduces changes to functional connectivity in anesthetized humans, exhibiting selective attenuation of matrix thalamocortical loops relative to core loops. Most importantly, the simulation identified a previously unknown biomarker of propofol concentration: elevated residual inter-stimulus cortical activity. This dose-dependent biomarker was subsequently confirmed in empirical macaque data, where it had previously gone unnoticed. This simulation-first discovery, arising from mechanistic circuit dynamics rather than statistical comparison of clinical populations, serves as an illustrative example of a broader generative framework that can translate receptor-level modulation into circuit-scale biomarkers with potential applications across predictive neuropharmacology.
items.authors: Pathak, A.; Brincat, S. L.; Xiong, Y.; Organtzidis, H.; Protter, M.; Du, V.; Strey, H. H.; Mujica-Parodi, L. R.; Miller, E. K.; Granger, R.

items.title: Robust brain inspired prediction of speech recognition accuracy across many words, voices, and natural background sounds
items.abstract: Although humans generally excel at recognizing speech in noisy natural environments, performance varies widely due to differences in the background acoustics and individual talker attributes such as voice quality, intonation, and pitch. The underlying neural and acoustic factors of this perceptual variability remain elusive, making it an unresolved challenge to predict when speech recognition will succeed or fail. Here, we characterize human speech recognition across a wide range of natural conditions using speech spoken by 326 diverse male and female talkers of multiple ages embedded in 33 unique background noises. Across this vast soundscape, speech recognition is strongly driven by the spectrum and modulation statistics of the noise. Yet, articulatory speech features - including fundamental and formant frequencies - exert categorically distinct modulatory effects on recognition accuracy across the talkers age and gender, and specific words. This perceptual variability is captured by a low-dimensional statistical representation of sounds based on computations that emulate intermediate stages of sound processing and feature extraction in auditory midbrain. A model utilizing these sound summary statistics accurately predicts individual listeners single-trial recognition behavior, accounting for performance variance across individual voices, words, and backgrounds. Thus, speech-in-noise perception across diverse natural conditions relies largely on a simple set of spectrotemporal summary statistics known to be represented by central neural populations. Significance StatementAlthough humans can easily maintain conversations amidst environmental noise and voice variations, this capacity is severely degraded by hearing impairment and challenges modern speech recognition technologies. This study evaluates human speech recognition across a broad spectrum of environmental noises and diverse speaker demographics. We show that a brain-inspired auditory representation of sounds extracts critical statistical sound features driving human behavior, precisely predicting variations in perceptual accuracy across distinct voices, words, and environmental backgrounds.
items.authors: Clonan, A. C.; Stevenson, I. H.; Escabi, M. A.
